wine.name: Vat 1 Semillon
wine.grapes: Semillon alone, from old, dry grown vines.
wine.sites: Old vine Semillon of the estate at Pokolbin, dry grown and on its own roots, with the Short Flat vineyard at its heart, where Semillon was planted in 1923 and 1927.
wine.making: Picked by hand and early, at low sugar, the fruit is pressed lightly and only the free run juice is fermented cool in stainless steel tanks. The wine rests about six weeks on its fine lees and is bottled in the winter after the harvest, with no oak at any stage.
wine.glass: Lemon juice, lemon peel and lime over a waxy, almost paraffin texture when young, light in body and quiet, with high, fresh acidity; with years in bottle come buttered toast, lanolin and honey, while the wine stays dry.
wine.ageing: Tight and lemony for its first few years, it begins to show toast and lanolin after five to ten years in bottle, and a strong vintage keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 7 to 10 degrees Celsius, an older bottle at the warmer end; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: A cellar code of the house, named for a vat, not a vineyard or a legal term.

records.table: Tyrrell's Vat 1 Semillon is Hunter Valley Semillon from old, dry grown vines at Pokolbin, picked early, fermented in steel and given no oak. Lemony and light when young, it turns to toast and lanolin with years in bottle, so pour an older one if you can.
records.story: The founder, an English emigrant who had come out in 1850, took up land at Pokolbin in 1858 and built a slab hut there; the house and the Australian Dictionary of Biography both date his first vintage to 1864. His son Dan Tyrrell (1871 to 1959) made his first wine in 1885, at fourteen, and his last in 1959, running the winery after his father's death in 1909 while a brother helped with the vines. Until then most of the wine was sold to other wineries. Murray Tyrrell (1921 to 2000), a grandson of the founder, took over in 1959 and began to keep the chosen wines for the family's own label. In the 1960s he set them apart as the Winemaker's Selection, each named for the vat or cask that held it, and Vat 1 was the Semillon. He planted Chardonnay in 1968, and its first wine, Vat 47 of 1971, is counted by the house as the first commercial varietal Chardonnay of Australia, a claim others have contested. Vat 1 kept to the old Hunter way: picked early, fermented in steel and never touched by oak, so that its toast and lanolin come from the bottle alone. For a sommelier it is the standing proof that a hot, humid valley can make a light, long lived dry white.

wine.name: Maurice O'Shea Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the estate's old vineyards.
wine.sites: Chosen parcels of the estate's old Pokolbin vineyards, above all Old Hill, planted in 1880 on volcanic soil beneath the Brokenback Range, Old Paddock, planted in 1921 from its cuttings on red volcanic loam, and Rosehill, planted in 1946.
wine.making: Drawn from the estate's chosen parcels and barrels, and made only in years the house judges strong enough, the wine is aged for about eighteen months in large French oak barrels before bottling.
wine.glass: Red cherry and violet when young, gaining the savoury notes of leather and turned earth that Hunter Shiraz takes on in bottle; medium in body and supple, with fine tannin, fresh acidity, a quiet frame of French barrels and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release yet built to last, it gains savoury depth over fifteen years and more, and a strong vintage keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Burgundy glass or a large red wine glass.

records.table: Mount Pleasant's Maurice O'Shea Shiraz honours the winemaker who made the estate's name between the 1920s and his death in 1956. Drawn from Pokolbin vineyards planted in 1880, 1921 and 1946, it is medium bodied and savoury, made only in strong years, and wants a decanter.
records.story: Shiraz has grown on the hill at Pokolbin since 1880, when an earlier settler planted the Old Hill vineyard on volcanic soil beneath the Brokenback Range. Maurice O'Shea (1897 to 1956) studied wine in France, at Montpellier and in Paris, and came home in 1920 at his mother's request. By the house's account the family bought the property in 1921, and he planted Old Paddock that year from cuttings of Old Hill; the Australian Dictionary of Biography dates the name Mount Pleasant to 1925. In the Depression, in 1932, he sold a half share to McWilliam's and stayed on as manager and winemaker, and in 1941 he sold the rest and went on making the wine. He planted Rosehill in 1946 and remained the estate's winemaker until his death in 1956. In 1987 the estate made the first Maurice O'Shea Shiraz, a selection drawn above all from Old Hill, Old Paddock and Rosehill, released in 1990 and bottled only in strong years. For a sommelier it ties O'Shea's name to the medium bodied, long lived Shiraz the Hunter is known for, from vines he planted or tended himself.

wine.name: Graveyard Vineyard Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the one vineyard.
wine.sites: The Graveyard Vineyard at Pokolbin, beside the house's first block, planted to Shiraz in 1968 on heavy clay, hard to work, which the house credits for the character of its fruit.
wine.making: Fermented in small open fermenters, the wine is matured for twelve to eighteen months, by vintage, in French oak. New French and American barriques once had a large share; the house has moved towards seasoned French puncheons and larger casks, with no new oak at all in 2022. In weak years the wine is declassified and not released as Graveyard.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and pomegranate with rose petal and a savoury edge when young, turning to leather and turned earth with age; medium in body, concentrated yet fine, with near silky tannin and a long line of acidity.
wine.ageing: Fragrant enough to drink young, it is built for the cellar: a strong vintage gains leather and savoury depth over decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Burgundy glass or a large red wine glass.

records.table: Brokenwood's Graveyard Vineyard Shiraz comes from a Pokolbin block marked on the parish map for a cemetery that was never used, planted to Shiraz in 1968. Fragrant and fine, with red cherry and rose petal, it ages for decades, and the house holds it back in weak years.
records.story: In 1970 three Sydney lawyers, who claimed little knowledge of viticulture, bought a small block at Pokolbin that had once been meant for a cricket ground. They planted Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon in 1971 and picked their first vintage in 1973. In 1978 six new partners joined the venture, which made it possible to buy the neighbouring vineyard, planted to Shiraz in 1968. It was called the Graveyard because the Pokolbin parish map marked it as the Cemetery Block, though it was never used as one. Its heavy clay was hard to work, but its fruit stood apart, and in 1983, the first vintage of a new winemaker, the house began to bottle its single vineyard wines, the Graveyard Shiraz among them. The partnership grew, yet the Graveyard stayed a wine of one site, and the house declassifies it in weak years: by the house's count of 2018, six of its first thirty five vintages were not sold under the name. For a sommelier it is Pokolbin Shiraz of one vineyard, fragrant and medium bodied, from a house that began as three lawyers' venture and became one of the names a guest knows in the Hunter.

wine.name: Lake's Folly Cabernets
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the greater part, with Shiraz, Merlot and Petit Verdot in shares that change with the year.
wine.sites: The estate's own single vineyard at Pokolbin, hand picked and low yielding; Block 1, the Cabernet planted in 1963, stands in front of the cellar door.
wine.making: The hand picked estate fruit is fermented in open fermenters, which its sellers credit with soft, fine tannin. The young wine settles for about six months in large old casks, then spends about a year in small French oak barriques, new, one and two years old, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and violet with a touch of eucalyptus, perfumed and light to medium in weight, with fine grained tannin, savoury French barrels in the background and a long, dry finish; more elegance than power.
wine.ageing: Perfumed and open in youth, it gains savoury depth over ten to twenty years in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Lake's Folly Cabernets is a Cabernet Sauvignon blend from one Pokolbin vineyard, first planted in 1963 by a Sydney surgeon's family in a valley of Semillon and Shiraz. Perfumed and light to medium in weight, with blackcurrant and violet, it suits a guest who wants elegance over power.
records.story: Max Lake (1924 to 2009) was a Sydney surgeon who specialised in surgery of the hand. In 1963 his family and friends planted Cabernet Sauvignon on a block at Pokolbin, in a valley known for Semillon and Shiraz, and the vines of that first planting, Block 1, stand in front of the cellar door. By the house's account the first vintage came in 1966, made by hand and foot, and Chardonnay followed in 1969. A small estate making wine from its own vines alone, Lake's Folly is often called the first boutique winery of modern Australia. The founder's son became its winemaker in 1982, with his father consulting, by the house's timeline. In early 2000 the family sold the estate to a Perth businessman, and the Cabernets comes from the same single vineyard. Its blend moves with the year, led by Cabernet Sauvignon, with Shiraz, Merlot and Petit Verdot beside it, and a guest remembers it for perfume and fine tannin rather than weight. For a sommelier it answers the guess that the Hunter grows only Semillon and Shiraz: Cabernet of restraint, from a surgeon's folly that lasted.

wine.name: Braemore Semillon
wine.sites: The Braemore vineyard on Hermitage Road, Pokolbin, planted in 1969 on a narrow band of deep, free draining sandy loam, alluvial soil laid down by an ancient watercourse.
wine.making: Hand picked, in some years passed over a sorting table, the fruit is pressed as whole bunches to keep phenolics low and fermented in stainless steel with a neutral yeast. The wine rests four to six weeks, by vintage, on its yeast lees and is bottled in the autumn after the harvest, with no oak.
wine.glass: Lemongrass, lime zest and chamomile with soft green herbs when young, light in body, with taut, high acidity and a long, dry finish; with years in bottle it gains toast, honey and lanolin.
wine.ageing: Bright and drinkable on release, it is built to age: the house holds some back as a Cellar Reserve, released with five to seven years in bottle, when the toast begins to show.
wine.serve: 7 to 10 degrees Celsius, an older bottle at the warmer end; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

records.table: Thomas Wines' Braemore Semillon comes from one Pokolbin vineyard planted in 1969 on deep alluvial sand. Whole bunch pressed and made in steel without oak, it is taut with lime and lemongrass when young; the Cellar Reserve shows the toast and honey that bottle age brings.
records.story: The Braemore vineyard was planted to Semillon in 1969 beside Hermitage Road at Pokolbin, on a narrow band of sandy alluvial soil laid down by an ancient watercourse. The house's founder grew up in McLaren Vale, the son of a winemaker there, and came to the Hunter in 1987 to join Tyrrell's, where he made wine for some thirteen years. In 1997 he released the first wine under his own name, choosing to make only the Hunter's two signature grapes, Semillon and Shiraz, and two years later he left Tyrrell's to set up on his own at Pokolbin. For the 2000 vintage the young house first bought Braemore fruit, and the single vineyard Semillon it made became its flagship white. It went on buying the fruit for nearly two decades, and in December 2017, when the vineyard's owners decided to sell, Thomas Wines bought Braemore outright. The wine keeps to the Hunter's old way, early picking, steel and no oak, and the house releases a Cellar Reserve of it with years in bottle. For a sommelier it is the modern face of Hunter Semillon: a single vineyard long in a grower's hands, made by a winemaker trained at Tyrrell's, and proof that the style carries on in new hands.

traps: Braemore is a vineyard on Hermitage Road that Thomas Wines bought in 2017; the house made its Braemore Semillon from bought fruit from the 2000 vintage on.
Braemore's toast and honey with age come from the bottle, not from oak; the wine is made in stainless steel.

cards.front: Thomas Wines' Braemore Semillon: what soil is the Braemore vineyard planted on?
cards.back: A narrow band of deep, free draining sandy loam, alluvial soil laid down by an ancient watercourse, on Hermitage Road at Pokolbin.

cards.front: When did Thomas Wines first make Braemore Semillon, and when did it buy the vineyard?
cards.back: It first bought Braemore fruit for the 2000 vintage and bought the vineyard in December 2017.

questions.q: A guest asks how Thomas Wines' Braemore Semillon is pressed and fermented. Which answer is right?
opts: Whole bunch pressed, fermented in stainless steel
Crushed with skin contact, fermented in new oak
Left a week on skins, fermented in amphora
Foot trodden, fermented in old oak puncheons
questions.exp: Braemore is whole bunch pressed to keep phenolics low and fermented in stainless steel with a neutral yeast; skin contact and new oak would blur the lean, lemony style the house is after.

questions.q: Where did the founder of Thomas Wines make wine from 1987 until he set up on his own at Pokolbin in 1999?
questions.exp: He joined Tyrrell's in 1987 and made wine there for some thirteen years before leaving in 1999; Brokenwood, Mount Pleasant and Lake's Folly are other Pokolbin houses.

sources.title: Gourmet Traveller Wine: Betting on Braemore

report: The founder is living and his surname is the house's; he is described, never named, and the read-together agent may add his name to people.json. The vineyard's former owners, who sold it in 2017, are living and not named.

The founding year is 1997 in the house's words and Wine Selectors, for the first wine; two accounts date the estate at Pokolbin to 1999, when he left Tyrrell's, so founded keeps 1997 and the story gives both.
The house puts the vineyard on a band of alluvial sandy loam formed by an ancient watercourse, while another of its pages speaks of an ancient sea floor; sites follows the watercourse.
Two accounts differ on who planted Braemore in 1969 (one names its long time owner, another a partnership of four who bought the land late in 1968), so the story names no planter.

The making rests on the house's notes for the 2023 and 2025 vintages (whole bunch pressed, stainless steel, neutral yeast, five or six weeks on lees, bottled in May); the glass on the same notes, with the aged notes the region's.

Alcohol runs from about ten and a half to twelve per cent by vintage in the house's notes, so the record gives none; Kiss Shiraz is sourced only as a wine of the house, so its note claims no more, and the Six Degrees Semillon of Braemore fruit is left out, its making known for one vintage only.

No swap proposed: Thomas Wines is younger than the other four houses, but two secondary sources call Braemore one of the region's celebrated single vineyard Semillons, and it gives the group a grower's vineyard beside the old family names.

changed: wine.making: five or six weeks on lees is now four to six weeks by vintage, since the 2019 notes give four and the 2014 six.
wine.ageing, label and others: the Cellar Reserve is released with five to seven years in bottle by the house's pages, not about six.
story and a question: rose to red winemaker is cut, found in one account of this check only; he made wine at Tyrrell's for some thirteen years.
story: a small parcel of Braemore fruit is cut, since no source gave the size of the first purchase.
open: The first Braemore of 2000 rests on two trade accounts (Gourmet Traveller Wine, The Shout); one Newcastle Herald account may imply a later start.
